Please see https://wiki.whatwg.org/wiki/FAQ#Is_there_a_process_for_adding_new_features_to_a_specification.3F

What use case is this solving? As far as I can tell it is only "as a developer, I prefer not writing script elements." It does not add any new platform capabilities, and indeed goes against the design of template as explicitly (per spec) a "script supporting element."

Can you start over, and per the wiki, avoid jumping to a solution? Start with the use cases. What are they? Are there other existing ways to solve them? If it helps, explicitly go through the steps listed there to guide your thinking.

Sorry, I thought it was obvious enough, but that's because it is already in my mind.

The use case would be clients that have javascript disabled. The suggestion that it would be a "script supporting element" is not accurate as it currently "requires" scripting.

If I could _only_ use the html specs by using script components, that would mean things are getting mixed up. I think there should be no constraints both ways, but that just 2 cents.

Also, I don't think it should be problems only, this is an opportunity and the use case (as summarized in the examples) could be applied to any type of document, no particular :-)

("Script supporting" means "exists to support JavaScript code". HTML and JavaScript are explicitly designed to work together, so things getting "mixed up" is actually a good thing.)

What type of site could potentially use a dynamic templating element without having JavaScript enabled? If no dynamic client-side information (via JavaScript) is possible, I see two potential types of pages:
1. Pages which display the same information to every visitor. These are obviously not templated, so the template element does not apply.
2. Pages which use server-side templating to customize what each visitor sees. These also do not need the template element, since they can (and should, for performance) do the templating on the server side.

As you can see, the template element was specifically designed to be used by script, and doesn't make sense in situations without script, including users who have disabled JavaScript.

Regardless, you still haven't worked with the steps I linked you to. "Users with JavaScript disabled" is not a use case. What do those users want to do? Please do not mention the template element or any other proposed _solution_ in your use case description. We are interested purely in the actual thing a user should be able to accomplish which they cannot today.

Thanks for your response, interesting points.

"Script supporting" could mean anything, but it does/should not mean "script only". By having such a "small" window of use, you also are limiting the windowsof oppurtunity (and imho the window of success). Mixing things up is good, I really like how templating + scripting is use by for example Polymer, but it shouldn't be a constraint to use the full spectrum of the html specification.

As for you two use cases, I think in both cases are valid for using html-only templating.
1. Templating could be used to keep consistency. For larger files with repeating elements it could also have some improvement of net performance due to smaller code footprint. It also has some kind of seperation between data and presentation. As for the concept of web components it helps with encapsulation if using several different basic components to build the complete output.
2. Also for serverside scripting above pro's are valid; keeping your view compact by re-using consistent (dynamic) templates would be a great improvement. Currently printing 100 rows is done by just outputting the same HTML 100 times. Also for using parts that repeat thru different pages (as navigation) it would be a welcome feature (currently this is done by including the same view over and over in every page, doing this thru a cached template would be much more interesting).

A lot of potential comes from the possibility to dynamic build the template. Currently there are no direct placeholders to insert data into it. Consequence is that 'data-placeholders' are looked up thru scripting (performance!). Adding these would make the use case for html templating much more attractive. As HTML is not dynamic by nature (as in control-statements) it would never have the flexibility as real scripting, but for a lot of cases it would still work out (for example passing different data from serverside logic). As for performance it comes down how it is implemented; if the template is 'compiled' once where the placeholders are dynamic parameters, I think it could become pretty performant ;-)

I can see why you say the element should be 'script supporting' as HTML will never cover all the cases you can solve with dynamic scripting, but limiting it to only that would be a waste as there are many oppurtinities left over.

_I hope my English is ok. I will surely go thru your steps asap and add it!_

So the HTML spec has actually had at least two declarative templating features in the past, but they haven't been successful.

https://whatwg.org/specs/web-forms/current-work/#repeatingFormControls
https://whatwg.org/specs/web-apps/2007-10-26/multipage/section-datatemplate.html

I think the main reason is that the needs for templating is very different for different applications, and so anything we come up with is only going to be useful for a (small?) subset of templating needs. The current setup that requires scripting to be used at all has the drawback that it can't be used without script, but has the benefit that it is usable for all scripted applications.

It seems to me that the `template` element has been successful. It's not clear to me why we should invest resources in trying to do declarative templating again when it has failed in the past.

@zcorpan If the arguments for failing also applies to the current situation, I would agree we'd have to foresee this. But I'm not sure what the reason for failure were - I didn't actually know those existed before you pointed me at it. Of course one will not succeed by counting one's failures.

The elements in the source file seem to be more like control-element/statements, that's not something I'd vote for. I'd say control structures need to be dynamic and so in (optional) scripting.

I agree on the great difference in uses for templating. But the same is for any other element in HTML. I'd like to see a nice HTML standard with optional scripting. I'm pro-scripting, but as an optional component. There are several reasons to this (some mentioned before): no possibility/need for using scripting (many reasons, parsers, e-mail,..), performance, browser implementation (caching simple templates), easier to understand, freedom of implementation, auto-complete on IDE's (more easier at least).

_Still have to go thru the links domenic gave, been busy, still hope to add it soon._

I'm sympathetic to it being nice to have declarative templating features that cover the most common use cases, but I think this needs research, design and demonstrated interest from browser vendors to implement before this is actionable for the HTML spec. So closing this issue for now.

If you want to work on this, I would recommend researching httparchive or some other big dataset for how the `template` element is used in the wild, and have a discussion with some people who implemented the `template` element in a browser engine (if they are interested).
